paper_title: Chiplet Multi-Objective Optimization Algorithm Based on Communication Consumption and Temperature

extraction.paper_title: Chiplet Multi-Objective Optimization Algorithm Based on Communication Consumption and Temperature

scenario.description: Multi-window display (MWD) system with 12 chiplets mapped on a 2.5-D IC with passive interposer. Initial layout compared against CMO algorithm results with varying weight factors (α=0.5, α=0.8, α=0.2) and single-objective optimization.
scenario.architecture: 2.5-D heterogeneous system on passive silicon interposer with 12 IP cores separated into chiplets; mesh topology network-on-chip; 6-layer stack including organic substrate, C4 bump layer, silicon interposer, microbump layer, chiplet layout, and thermal interface material (TIM); air-forced heatsink with fin-channel design (fin-height 30 mm, fin-width 1 mm, fan radius 10 cm, 5000 RPM).
scenario.workload: Multi-window display multimedia application with task-based communication graph; communication volumes range from 64–256 Mbit/s between chiplets per Table 1.
scenario.operating_point: Ambient temperature 318.5 K; steady-state thermal analysis using Hotspot 7.0 with fourth-order Runge-Kutta solver.

original_setup.solver: Hotspot 7.0 fourth-order Runge Kutta with adaptive step sizing
original_setup.optimizer: Chiplet Multi-Objective Optimization (CMO) algorithm with communication and temperature heuristic information and weight factor α
original_setup.controller: Weight factor α (0 ≤ α ≤ 1) to balance communication consumption minimization (α=0.8) versus temperature minimization (α=0.2); α=0.5 shown as baseline multi-objective result
original_setup.benchmark: Multi-window display (MWD) multimedia SoC with 12 IP cores separated into 12 chiplets mapped on 2.5-D passive interposer; initial layout versus CMO algorithm layouts with three α values (0.5, 0.8, 0.2) and single-objective optimization comparison

thermal_observable.location: peak maximum temperature across entire 2.5-D system (chiplet array on interposer)
thermal_observable.aggregation: steady-state maximum temperature from Hotspot thermal map output

physical_mismatches.reason: Passive interposer architecture with microbumps and TSVs differs fundamentally from monolithic 2-D designs; chiplet-to-chiplet communication via interposer induces latency and power not modeled in simplified heuristic mappings

Heuristic information calculation (Equations 1-2) uses Manhattan distance on uniform grid topology, but actual 2.5-D thermal coupling through silicon interposer and package is 3-D with anisotropic thermal resistance matrix computed by Hotspot; grid-based approximation does not capture full thermal physics

Algorithm assumes even power distribution across each chiplet and uniform surface temperature per chiplet [29], but actual power density and thermal gradients within heterogeneous chiplets vary significantly; simplification validated only by correlation with Hotspot post-hoc

Theoretical chiplet sizes include spacing as preprocessing (e.g., chiplet_blend actual 2.5×2.5 mm mapped to theoretical 4.0×4.0 mm), but interposer thermal model in Hotspot uses actual chiplet dimensions (Table 2); mismatch between mapping grid and Hotspot thermal geometry

Algorithm optimizes communication wirelength on mesh topology and thermal placement heuristic; no explicit thermal controller or dynamic frequency/voltage scaling modeled; system operates at fixed ambient 318.5 K with fixed fan speed 5000 RPM
Thermal transient dynamics modeled by Hotspot but algorithm produces only steady-state optimal layouts; no time-dependent optimization or thermal cycling analysis

studio_assumptions: Power evenly distributed over each chiplet surface with uniform chiplet temperature [29]
Chiplet thinness and high thermal conductivity justify surface temperature equals bulk temperature assumption
Chiplet theoretical sizes preprocessed to include mandatory spacing; grid occupancy encodes both chiplet and minimum inter-chiplet gap constraints
Manhattan distance between chiplet centers (via midpoints of occupied grid regions) used as proxy for 3-D thermal and communication coupling
Energy per bit (Ebit) per unit distance constant at 0.186 (from line 6 in Algorithm 3: `cost[i][j] × 0.186`)
Weight factor α linearly combines normalized heuristic information via min-max scaling (Equation 3); no nonlinear temperature-communication trade-off model
Hotspot 7.0 thermal resistance matrix computed once for fixed geometry; no feedback from algorithm-generated layout back to Hotspot during optimization (post-hoc validation only)
Communication task graph (Figure 2, Table 1) static and known; no runtime workload variation or load migration between chiplets
Organic substrate FR-4, silicon interposer, microbump interconnects, and TIM properties fixed per Hotspot default 2.5-D model; no sensitivity analysis or material variation
Symmetry reduction of initial node search (Section 3.2.2, Algorithm 1) assumes grid topology symmetry yields identical layouts; no asymmetric thermal or power asymmetries considered in reduction
missing_inputs: No repository link or supplementary code archive provided; CMO algorithm implementation in C++ not publicly available for verification

Specific Hotspot configuration file (.config) and material thermal properties (thermal conductivity, specific heat, density for silicon, interposer dielectric, organic substrate, TIM, spreader, heatsink) not included; default Hotspot 7.0 parameters assumed but not documented
Chiplet placement coordinates and final layout geometry for CMO result (Figure 9b, α=0.5) not tabulated; only thermal map image provided without numeric floorplan

Single-objective optimization baseline [31] algorithm details from reference [31] ('New Heuristic Algorithm for Low Energy Mapping for 2.5-D Integration', Electronics 2022, 11, 1817) not included in packet; comparison method unspecified
Energy-per-bit constant Ebit=0.186 (Algorithm 3, line 6) source and units not explained; assumed derived from ORION 2.0 [30] but conversion factor and NoC architecture specifics not provided
Temperature and communication heuristic normalization bounds (ηi1_min, ηi1_max, ηi2_min, ηi2_max in Equation 3, Algorithm 3) computed during algorithm execution but not reported for reproducibility
Hotspot 7.0 transient solver parameters (time step, convergence tolerance, thermal capacitance model) not specified; only Runge-Kutta method name given

Chiplet functional specifications (e.g., CPU, memory, I/O core types for mem3, hs, nr, in, vs, mem2, hvs, jug1, jug2, se, mem1, blend) not detailed; power values in Table 2 assumed constant but duty cycle and temporal variation unknown

MWD multimedia application workload trace or reference [28] ('Chip-set for video display of multimedia information', IEEE Trans. Consum. Electron. 1999, 45, 706–715) communication patterns not provided; static task graph may not represent peak thermal scenarios

Heatsink fin geometry (30 mm height, 1 mm width) and fan model (10 cm radius, 5000 RPM forced convection) not validated against standard thermal test conditions; air velocity, pressure drop, and heat transfer coefficient not independently specified

methods.note: The paper claims to optimize chiplet placement for 2.5-D IC via a multi-objective heuristic algorithm (CMO) that minimizes temperature and communication consumption simultaneously. However, the heuristic information calculation (Equations 1–2) uses Manhattan distance on a uniform grid topology as proxy for 3-D thermal coupling, which is fundamentally incompatible with the 3-D thermal resistance matrix computed by Hotspot. The grid topology represents chiplets as occupying integer node counts with preprocessed theoretical sizes (Table 2: e.g., blend actual 2.5×2.5 mm → theoretical 4.0×4.0 mm), but Hotspot receives actual chiplet geometries. This mismatch invalidates the claimed optimization—the algorithm optimizes relative to a simplified 2-D mesh model, not the actual 3-D steady-state thermal field that Hotspot computes. The paper acknowledges power uniformity assumption [29] but does not reconcile grid-based distance metrics with continuous 3-D thermal physics.

code.note: No C++ implementation, Hotspot configuration file (.config), or supplementary code archive provided. Paper states 'The algorithm uses C++ language to verify its validity and accuracy' (Section 4) but no source code, pseudocode beyond Algorithms 1–3, or executable is available. Algorithm 3 (Heuristic information calculation) contains undefined variable references (e.g., 'D[map[k]]' syntax appears corrupted on line 13: 'temcost+=power[mapp[i]]/D[map[i]]D[map[k]];' lacks operator between two D[] terms). Reproducibility of CMO mapping and heuristic computation impossible without corrected, executable code.

parameters.note: Chiplet power values (Table 2) are stated as constant (e.g., nr: 70 W, hs: 40 W) with no justification of duty cycle, temporal variation, or peak power. The assumption that 'power is evenly distributed over the chiplet' and 'surface temperature...is consistent with the overall temperature' [29] contradicts heterogeneous chiplet function (CPU, memory, I/O cores have different thermal properties and transient behavior). Communication volume in Table 1 is also static (256–64 Mbit/s); no runtime workload variation or thermal hotspot migration modeled. Heuristic normalization bounds (ηi1_min, ηi1_max, ηi2_min, ηi2_max in Equation 3, Algorithm 3) are computed during execution but never reported, precluding verification of the normalized heuristic values or α-weighting impact. Energy-per-bit constant Ebit = 0.186 (Algorithm 3, line 6) lacks units and source derivation—assumed to convert communication volume × distance to energy, but scaling and units unspecified relative to stated Mbit/s and grid node distance.

config.note: Hotspot 7.0 thermal configuration file (.config) and material properties not provided. Paper specifies heatsink dimensions (fin-height 30 mm, fin-width 1 mm, fan 10 cm radius, 5000 RPM) and ambient 318.5 K, but does not document thermal conductivity, specific heat, or density for silicon interposer, organic substrate FR-4, microbumps, TSVs, TIM, spreader, or heatsink material. Thermal resistance and capacitance matrix entries computed by Hotspot are architecture-level abstractions that depend on these material parameters and layer stack geometry. Without .config file and material specs, Hotspot setup cannot be replicated. Transient solver parameters (time step, convergence tolerance) mentioned only by method name ('fourth-order Runge Kutta with adaptive step sizing'); numerical values not given.

data.note: Chiplet placement coordinates for CMO result (Figure 9b, α=0.5) not tabulated; only thermal map image provided. Extraction floorplan assumed layout from Figure 3 schematic and Table 2 sizes, inferring positions to match visual 8×8 grid shown, but actual node-to-coordinate mapping produced by CMO algorithm is unverified and unvalidated against the paper's claimed 373.58 K peak temperature. Single-objective optimization baseline [31] algorithm details and comparison method unspecified—reference [31] ('New Heuristic Algorithm for Low Energy Mapping for 2.5-D Integration', Electronics 2022, 11, 1817) is a different 2023 work by subset of same authors but not included in packet. Communication task graph (Figure 2, Table 1) static; no runtime trace or scenario variability provided. Hotspot temperature results (thermal map images in Figure 9) are visual outputs; underlying numeric temperature matrix not tabulated per chiplet or per spatial grid point, preventing independent validation of peak temperature claims (381.41 K, 373.58 K, 377.36 K, 371.94 K) or temperature distribution profiles.

findings.reason: Algorithm computes heuristic information η using Manhattan distance on uniform 2-D grid topology (Equations 1–2, Algorithms 2–3), but Hotspot solves 3-D transient heat diffusion through multi-layer passive interposer stack with anisotropic thermal resistance. Grid node distance is 1-D or 2-D approximation; actual thermal coupling between chiplets depends on 3-D paths through interposer, microbumps, TSVs, spreader, and heatsink. Temperature-based heuristic ηi2 = Σ Pj / di,j assumes linear thermal superposition with 1/distance decay, which is valid in unbounded 2-D or 3-D media but not in confined package geometry with boundary layers. Hotspot thermal resistance matrix encodes full 3-D geometry; heuristic does not.
findings.locator: Pages 7–8, Equations 1–2, Algorithms 2–3; Section 3.2.4 'Computing Heuristic Information and Mapping Chiplets'; Hotspot specification pages 2–3 'creating a circuit model for heat dissipation' via 'thermal resistance/capacitance values' for stacked architecture. Fundamental incompatibility: grid heuristic optimizes topology; Hotspot validates 3-D solution post-hoc without algorithmic feedback.

findings.reason: Chiplet theoretical sizes (Table 2) incorporate mandatory spacing into grid occupancy (e.g., chiplet_blend actual 2.5×2.5 mm + spacing = theoretical 4.0×4.0 mm occupying 2×2 grid nodes at unit grid size). However, Hotspot thermal model receives actual chiplet dimensions from paper parameters, not theoretical sizes. Distance calculation in algorithm uses grid node spacing; Hotspot uses Euclidean coordinates in millimeters. Section 3.2.4 and Figure 7 explain that Manhattan distance between chiplet centers is approximated via grid midpoints, but conversion factor between grid units and millimeters is never specified. Algorithm generates mappings on normalized grid; Hotspot evaluates on actual mm-scale geometry—mismatch propagates through entire optimization.
findings.locator: Pages 4–5, Table 2, text 'theoretical size...actual size plus the distance'; page 9, Figure 7, text 'Manhattan distance between the midpoints'; Section 3.2.4, Equations 1–2 using di,j without unit definition. Chiplet_blend example: actual 2.5 mm assumed to occupy grid nodes, but grid cell width not stated; unit mismatch between algorithm and simulator.

findings.reason: Paper assumes power uniformly distributed over each chiplet and surface temperature equals bulk temperature [29]. This uniform temperature assumption contradicts heterogeneous chiplet function and contradicts Hotspot's thermal resistance network, which models temperature gradients across layer stack and within chiplets. Assumption is simplification for heuristic design, but algorithm does not compute or iterate on actual chiplet-internal temperature distribution—it treats each chiplet as isothermal point source for heuristic weight. Hotspot solves full conduction problem and will show intra-chiplet gradients not captured in algorithm; optimization based on point heuristic will not guarantee isothermal chiplet assumption in actual layout.
findings.locator: Page 4, Section 3.2, Table 2 text 'we assume that the power is evenly distributed over the chiplet' and 'surface temperature...is consistent with the overall temperature. [29]'; Page 3, Hotspot description 'creating a circuit model for the heat dissipation within a microprocessor's different architecture-level blocks', indicating node-level temperature nodes, not chiplet-uniform.

findings.reason: Algorithm 3, line 13 contains syntax error: 'temcost+=power[mapp[i]]/D[map[i]]D[map[k]];' lacks operator between 'D[map[i]]' and 'D[map[k]]'. This appears to be missing multiplication or addition. If multiplication intended, equation reads: temcost += power[mapp[i]] / (D[map[i]] * D[map[k]]), but indices are unclear (mapp vs map, D index semantics undefined). Variable mapp vs map inconsistency unresolved. Code cannot be executed or verified as written.

Equation 3 normalizes heuristic information using min-max scaling with bounds ηi1_min, ηi1_max, ηi2_min, ηi2_max, described as 'maximum and minimum heuristic factors' (Algorithm 3 input list). These bounds are computed during algorithm execution as heuristics are evaluated over all candidate nodes, but paper never reports actual numerical values for any layout (initial, α=0.5, α=0.8, α=0.2). Without these bounds, the normalized heuristic values ηi and combined weight cannot be computed or validated. Verification of α=0.5 balance between communication and temperature terms is impossible.
findings.locator: Page 8, Equation 3 and Algorithm 3 lines 16–17, input specification: 'maximum and minimum heuristic factors, ηi_min^1, ηi_max^1, ηi_min^2, ηi_max^2'; Section 3.2.4 text 'normalized using min-max scaling'. Paper provides final results (Figure 9, 10) but not intermediate heuristic values or normalization bounds.

findings.reason: Algorithm 3, line 6 uses constant 0.186: 'comcost+=D[i][j] × cost[i][j] × 0.186;'. This constant is never defined or dimensioned in paper. Assumed to represent energy per bit per unit distance (Ebit in Equation 1), but units and derivation missing. Paper references ORION 2.0 [30] ('ORION 2.0: A fast and accurate NoC power and area model for early-stage design space exploration') for energy model, but conversion from ORION NoC power model to 2.5-D chiplet interposer Ebit is not explained. Constant 0.186 may be NoC-specific parameter that does not apply to direct chiplet-to-chiplet communication via passive interposer; use unjustified.
findings.locator: Page 8, Algorithm 3, line 6: 'comcost+=D[i][j] × cost[i][j] × 0.186;'; Page 1, reference [30] to ORION 2.0; Section 3.2.4, Equation 1 defines Ebit but does not assign numerical value or justify 0.186.

findings.reason: Communication priority list (Table 1, Figure 2) is static and based on average communication volume (64–256 Mbit/s) between chiplets. No runtime workload variation, thermal transient dynamics, or per-frame communication pattern provided. Algorithm assumes this static communication graph throughout execution and layout generation. However, multimedia applications (multi-window display) typically exhibit time-varying communication demand per output frame or scene. Peak thermal scenario may not coincide with static average communication graph used in optimization. Layout optimized for static graph may be suboptimal for actual dynamic workload.
findings.locator: Pages 3–4, Section 3.2.1, Table 1 'Communication priority list', Figure 2 communication task graph; reference [28] to MWD benchmark is 1999 IEEE Trans. Consum. Electron. paper on video display chipset, but detailed workload trace not included in packet.

findings.reason: Section 4 comparison includes 'single-objective optimization [31] result, which optimizes the communication consumption only' (Figure 9e, page 10). Reference [31] is cited as 'New Heuristic Algorithm for Low Energy Mapping for 2.5-D Integration', Electronics 2022, 11, 1817, a different paper by subset of same authors. Algorithm details, exact optimization objective, constraints, and mapping method for [31] baseline not documented in supplied packet. Without understanding of [31] algorithm, comparison fairness and reproducibility of Figure 9e result cannot be assessed. Baseline result could be from different CMO variant, different solver, or different problem formulation entirely.
findings.locator: Page 10, Section 4, Figure 9e caption and text 'single-objective optimization [31] result'; reference [31] Sun et al., Electronics 2022, 11, 1817, not included in packet.

findings.reason: Hotspot temperature results presented as thermal map visualizations in Figure 9 (pages 10–11) with stated peak temperatures: initial 381.41 K, CMO α=0.5: 373.58 K, α=0.8: 377.36 K, α=0.2: 371.94 K. Numeric values cited in text but underlying Hotspot output matrix (temperature at each spatial node or chiplet) not provided. Color-mapped Figure 9 images do not permit independent verification of peak temperature extraction or spatial distribution. Without numeric thermal data, temperature values cannot be cross-checked or recomputed from different visualization or interpolation methods.
findings.locator: Pages 10–11, Section 4 'Evaluation Results', Figure 9 (a)–(e) thermal map images, text 'The temperature is 381.41 K' (initial), 'maximum temperature drops to 373.58 K' (α=0.5), 'peak temperature is 377.36 K' (α=0.8), 'temperature is 371.94 K' (α=0.2).

findings.reason: CMO algorithm generates final layout for α=0.5 result (Figure 9b, claimed peak 373.58 K, communication 794.59 uJ). Paper shows thermal map visualization but does not provide chiplet placement coordinates (x, y positions on interposer). Extraction floorplan inferred from assumptions about grid layout and Table 2 sizes, but actual CMO output mapping (which nodes each chiplet occupies) never documented. Section 4 states 'different layouts derived from the algorithm will be compared', implying multiple layouts generated, but only final thermal maps shown. Intermediate and final floorplans not tabulated; reproducibility of exact layout and Hotspot input geometry impossible.
findings.locator: Page 10, Section 4, Figure 9(b) labeled 'multi-objective optimization result with α equal to 0.5' but no accompanying floorplan or coordinate table; Algorithms 1–3 produce layout on grid topology, but mapping output not reported.

findings.reason: Hotspot 7.0 thermal model requires detailed layer stack parameters: thermal conductivity (W/m·K) and specific heat (J/kg·K) for silicon, silicon dioxide, copper, organic substrate (FR-4), thermal interface material (TIM), spreader material, heatsink material; layer thicknesses; via dimensions and density. Paper specifies high-level Hotspot config (ambient 318.5 K, spreader 5 mm, heatsink 20 mm, fin-height 30 mm, fin-width 1 mm, fan 5000 RPM) but does not provide .config file or material table. Hotspot default parameters (from Hotspot 7.0 distribution) are assumed, but these defaults may not match 2.5-D passive interposer architecture described in paper. Without material properties, thermal resistance matrix cannot be independently computed or validated.
findings.locator: Page 3, Section 3.1 'Thermal Module Establishment', text specifies 'six layers...organic substrate, controlled collapse chip connection layer (C4 bump layer), silicon interposer, microbump layer, chiplet layout, and thermal interface material (TIM)' and Hotspot config parameters (318.5 K, spreader, heatsink, fin, fan), but no material properties or .config file content provided. Figure 1 shows schematic but no thickness or material labels on layers.

findings.reason: Paper states Hotspot uses 'fourth-order Runge Kutta algorithm with adaptive step sizing' (page 3) to solve transient differential equations, but does not specify numerical integration parameters: initial time step, adaptive refinement criteria, convergence tolerance for temperature, maximum number of iterations, simulation end time. These parameters impact numerical accuracy and convergence of thermal transient solution. Since paper claims steady-state optimization, transient solver output should be converged to steady-state; convergence criteria and end-time not specified. Reproducibility requires these Hotspot solver settings.
findings.locator: Page 3, Section 3.1, text 'To solve the transient differential equations, Hotspot uses a fourth-order Runge Kutta algorithm with adaptive step sizing.' findings.reason: Abstract and Section 4 claim 'peak temperature reduced by 8.34 K' for CMO α=0.5 result. Numeric values given: initial 381.41 K, optimized 373.58 K. Difference: 381.41 − 373.58 = 7.83 K, not 8.34 K. Abstract also claims 'communication power consumption reduced by 232.13 uJ'. Values given: initial 1026.72 uJ, optimized 794.59 uJ. Difference: 1026.72 − 794.59 = 232.13 uJ (correct). Temperature reduction arithmetic error suggests either typo in abstract/paper text, or initial/optimized temperature values inconsistent. Claimed 8.34 K reduction does not match stated 381.41 K → 373.58 K transition (7.83 K).
findings.locator: Page 1, Abstract: 'peak temperature reduced by 8.34 K and communication power consumption reduced by 232.13 µJ'; Page 10, Section 4: 'The maximum temperature drops to 373.58 K' from initial 381.41 K. Arithmetic: 381.41 − 373.58 = 7.83 K ≠ 8.34 K.

findings.reason: Paper introduces weight factor α (0 ≤ α ≤ 1) to balance communication (α→1) and temperature (α→0) objectives, but tests only three discrete values (α=0.5, 0.8, 0.2) and one single-objective baseline. No Pareto frontier or tradeoff curve (temperature vs. communication consumption) generated across full α range. This limits understanding of optimization landscape, dominance relationships, and designer's choice of α. Whether α=0.5 is truly optimal multi-objective solution (e.g., minimizing sum of normalized metrics) or merely an arbitrary choice is unclear. No sensitivity analysis of α impact on both objectives simultaneously.
findings.locator: Pages 7–8, Section 3.2.4, text 'weight α (0 ≤ α ≤ 1)...If the desired algorithm result is more focused on minimizing communication power consumption, α should take a larger value...if the desired algorithm result is more focused on minimizing temperature, α will take a smaller value. The designer can adjust α according to different requirements, and α = 0.5 is taken for calculation in this example.' Pages 10–11, Section 4, results reported for α=0.5, 0.8, 0.2, but no continuous curve or Pareto analysis.

findings.reason: Paper claims 2.5-D steady-state thermal analysis via Hotspot, which correctly models 3-D multi-layer stack with transient solver. However, extraction scenario marked 'steady_2d_relevant: true' is contradictory. The system is explicitly 3-D (passive interposer stack, TSVs, C4 bumps, thermal interface), not 2-D. Steady-state is correct (Hotspot converges transient to steady under constant power), but '2D' label implies monolithic 2-D IC without interposer, which is false. This is a descriptor mislabeling, not a technical error in the paper, but indicates extraction confusion about system dimensionality. Paper correctly addresses 2.5-D/3-D architecture; extraction categorization incorrect.
findings.locator: Extraction metadata: scenario.steady_2d_relevant=true vs. paper title 'Chiplet Multi-Objective Optimization Algorithm Based on...2.5-D IC' and page 1 'A chiplet multi-objective optimization algorithm for 2.5-D integrated circuit (IC) based on a passive interposer'. System is 3-D, not 2-D.

assessment.summary: Studio 2D steady-state screening label: **ILLUSTRATIVE_2D_ONLY (FAILED GATE)**. Studio did NOT run thermal simulation. Paper scenario describes a 2.5-D heterogeneous chiplet system on a passive silicon interposer with 12 cores optimized via the Chiplet Multi-Objective (CMO) algorithm balancing communication energy and peak temperature. Reported results (Table 2, Figure 9, α=0.5) show peak temperature 373.58 K with communication consumption 794.59 µJ, compared to initial layout baseline 381.41 K and 1026.72 µJ. Floorplan extraction from Table 2 reveals fatal geometric conflicts: chiplet mem1 (position [0.0255 m, 0 m], size 4.5×1.5 mm) and blend (position [0.0255 m, 0.0015 m], size 2.5×2.5 mm) both occupy the right region and overlap with jug2 (position [0.021 m, 0 m], size 4.5×4.5 mm). These overlaps violate physical realizability and prevent deterministic thermal simulation. The passive interposer architecture, 3-D thermal coupling via silicon and package, and grid-based Manhattan distance heuristics impose essential mismatches between CMO algorithm's simplified placement model and Hotspot's full 3-D resistor network. Numerical comparison is blocked by simulation infeasibility; qualitative sensitivity analysis indicates heuristic temperature prediction (Equations 1–2) does not capture anisotropic vertical heat spreading or microbump TSV thermal bottlenecks.
limitations: Geometric overlap in extracted floorplan: mem1 and blend conflict with jug2 placement, causing input validation gate failure and blocking Studio thermal execution.

Chiplet placement coordinates for CMO optimized layout (Figure 9b, α=0.5) not provided numerically; only thermal map image available, making post-hoc geometry reconstruction ambiguous and error-prone.

Manhattan distance heuristic (Equations 1–2) assumes uniform 2-D grid topology but ignores 3-D anisotropic thermal resistance through silicon interposer, microbump layers, and package substrate; grid-based cost does not reflect actual thermal paths.

Algorithm assumes uniform power distribution and single bulk temperature per chiplet [Ref. 29], contradicting heterogeneous power density (nr 70 W, blend 5 W) and thermal gradients within multi-core chiplets; simplification not validated independent of Hotspot post-hoc.
Heuristic normalization bounds (ηi1_min/max, ηi2_min/max) computed during algorithm execution but not reported; reproducibility of Equation 3 scaling undefined without these thresholds.
Energy-per-bit constant Ebit=0.186 (Algorithm 3, line 6) origin and units unexplained; assumed from ORION 2.0 [Ref. 30] but conversion factor and NoC mesh topology specifics unspecified.

No feedback between algorithm layout generation and Hotspot thermal model during optimization; CMO operates independently and Hotspot validates post-hoc only, preventing closed-loop temperature prediction.

Hotspot 7.0 solver parameters (time step, adaptive tolerance, thermal capacitance discretization) not documented; fourth-order Runge-Kutta method identified but convergence and stability assumptions not validated.
Single-objective baseline algorithm [Ref. 31] details omitted; comparison against prior art requires access to reference implementation for fair numerical and algorithmic assessment.

Symmetric layout reduction heuristic (Section 3.2.2, Algorithm 1) assumes grid symmetry yields identical results but does not account for asymmetric power distribution (nr 70 W vs. blend 5 W), invalidating symmetry assumption for heterogeneous systems.

Physical mismatch: passive interposer with discrete chiplets and TSVs introduces chip-to-chip communication latency and power overhead not modeled in heuristic wirelength cost; simplified Manhattan metric conflates NoC and thermal coupling.

Workload static; no transient thermal analysis or dynamic task migration modeled despite Hotspot capability; CMO produces time-independent layouts for fixed communication graph not accounting for runtime variability.

Material properties (silicon, interposer dielectric, TIM, heatsink fin-channel) fixed per Hotspot defaults without sensitivity study; fin geometry (30 mm height, 1 mm width, 5000 RPM fan) not independently validated against thermal test standards.
